food.text: The 20th century brought a revolution in American cooking. New technologies, the World Wars, a scientific understanding of food and continued immigration combined to create a wide range of new foods, giving the country a rich diversity of dishes.
The popularity of the automobile in the 20th century changed how Americans ate. It gave rise to drive-in and drive-through restaurants, which influenced American eating habits.

The expression 'soul food' originated in the mid-1960s, when 'soul' was a common word used to describe Black American culture. The cuisine began in the American South among enslaved Africans transported from Africa through the Atlantic slave trade. It started when enslaved people learned to make do with what their enslavers gave them to eat: leftovers and the undesirable parts of animals, such as ham hocks, hog jowls and pigs' feet, ears, skin, and intestines. It was initially denigrated as low-class food, but later became a primary source of pride in the African American community.

In 1941, the Food and Nutrition Board of the National Academy of Sciences established the first set of 'Recommended Dietary Allowances.' In 1943, the US War Food Administration issued War Food Order No. 1, which made enriched bread the law of the land.

From 1919 until Prohibition was repealed in 1933, many Italian-Americans struggled to keep their vineyards going. Some stayed in business by providing sacramental wine to the Catholic Church or grape juice to the general market. These holdouts are credited with salvaging America's viticulture heritage.

Frybread, a post-contact food, has become customary and even iconic at present-day Indigenous American social gatherings. Contemporary native peoples keep a varied culture of traditional foods while adding some foods that arrived after contact with Europeans.

The first documented sale of pierogi in America was made at the Marton House Tavern in Cleveland, Ohio, in 1928. After World War II, freshly cooked pierogi became a staple of fundraisers by ethnic churches. By the 1960s they were a common frozen supermarket item in the United States and Canada.

The California roll has been influential in sushi's global popularity. Its invention is often credited to a Japanese-born chef working in Los Angeles, with dates given as 1973 or even 1964. Some purist sushi chefs have snubbed it, and one scholar likened it to the American-born chop suey.
Carbonara is popular in the United States, yet it is unrecorded in Italy before World War II. Its origins may be due to an American influence connected to the allied liberation of Rome in 1944.

The National Council of Negro Women produced its first cookbook, The Historical Cookbook of the American Negro, in 1958. It revived the practice in 1993 with a popular series of cookbooks featuring recipes by famous Black Americans. Cookbooks like these helped fund the organization's charitable work.
tags: The Historical Cookbook of the American Negro

food.text: Since the mid-20th century, Black Americans have seasoned cooked meats and vegetables with Lawry's Seasoned Salt. It is economical and offers multiple herbs and spices in one product, so it is used in most dishes except sweet ones. By the mid-20th century, many were also turning to store-bought hot sauces.

Maria Gentile's The Italian Cook Book: The Art of Eating Well, published in New York in 1919, was a post-World War I effort to popularize Italian cooking in the United States. Italian-American food is now one of the top three cuisines in the country, according to the National Restaurant Association.

art.text: At an art show in New York in 1917, Marcel Duchamp presented a white porcelain urinal signed R. Mutt as a work of art. This made him the father of the "readymade". Duchamp and Francis Picabia were exploring similar anti-art notions at the same time Dada began in Zurich.

In July 2019, the 20th-Century Architecture of Frank Lloyd Wright was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list. It was the first time that modern American architecture had been recognized by UNESCO, and the 24th listing in the United States.

Mid-century modern design gained most of its popularity in North America, Brazil and Europe from roughly 1945 to 1970. It is characterized by clean, simple lines and a lack of decorative embellishment.

Visual arts by Indigenous peoples of the Americas include pottery, paintings, jewelry, weavings, sculptures, basketry, carvings and beadwork. Because too many artists posed as Native Americans to profit from the cachet of Indigenous art, the U.S. passed the Indian Arts and Crafts Act of 1990.
tags: Indian Arts and Crafts Act of 1990

art.text: The Guggenheim Museum was completed in 1959, although Frank Lloyd Wright's design for it had begun in the 1940s. It was the last of the eight Wright buildings in the World Heritage Site to be completed, and Wright died the same year.

George Gershwin and Ira Gershwin created Rhapsody in Blue in 1924, An American in Paris in 1928, and Porgy and Bess in 1935. These works are listed among the notable American stage and musical achievements of the twentieth century.
Palm Springs became a showcase for mid-century modern architecture. Albert Frey designed Palm Springs City Hall with Clark and Chambers between 1952 and 1957, and later built Frey House II in 1963.
The architect E. Stewart Williams designed a house for Frank Sinatra in 1946 that featured a piano-shaped pool. It is one of several mid-century modern landmarks in the Palm Springs area.

The Native Arts and Cultures Foundation was established in 2007 as a national foundation. The Ford Foundation, arts advocates and American Indian tribes created an endowment seed fund to support American Indian, Alaska Native and Native Hawaiian arts and cultures.

The Museum of Russian Art in Minneapolis was founded by collectors Raymond and Susan Johnson, who own the largest collection of Russian Realist paintings outside the former Soviet Union. Opened at its present location in 2005, it once hosted exhibitions ranging from Masterpieces of Soviet Era Painting to Faberge and nesting dolls.

The first UNESCO nomination of Wright's buildings was declined in July 2016 and referred back to the Frank Lloyd Wright Building Conservancy for revision. Eight buildings were re-nominated in December 2018, and the Price Tower and the Marin County Civic Center were excluded from the updated proposal.

Manowar has numerous releases referencing Norse mythology, including the 2007 concept album Gods of War. Its songs include Gates of Valhalla from Into Glory Ride in 1983 and Thor (The Powerhead) from Sign of the Hammer in 1984.

war.text: The United States entered World War I on April 6, 1917, more than two and a half years after the war began in Austria-Hungary. Until then, American public opinion had generally reflected a desire to stay out of the war.
war.source_title: American entry into World War I
tags: American entry into World War I

war.text: The United States initially had a small army, but after the Selective Service Act it drafted 2.8 million men. By summer 1918 it was sending 10,000 fresh soldiers to France every day.

Because the Americas were far from the central theaters of conflict, the threat of an Axis invasion of the continental United States was negligible, and the American theater saw relatively little fighting. Even so, it saw real killing: U-boats torpedoed ships within sight of East Coast cities, and in the Battle of the St. Lawrence residents on the Gaspé coast watched ships burn and explosions rattle their communities while bodies and debris floated ashore. In the Aleutian Islands campaign, 43 Americans were killed at Dutch Harbor, and on Attu the Japanese killed Charles Jones after interrogating him and sent Etta Jones and the Aleut population to Japan, where 16 of the Aleuts died. At Newfoundland, the ferry SS Caribou was torpedoed and sunk, and 137 of the 251 people aboard lost their lives.
war.source_title: American theater of World War II

war.text: Americans increasingly came to see Imperial Germany as the aggressor, especially after reports of German atrocities in Belgium in 1914. On May 7, 1915, a submarine of the Imperial German Navy torpedoed the British liner RMS Lusitania off the southern coast of Ireland and sank her, killing 1,199 civilians, including 128 US citizens. The sinking of a large, unarmed passenger ship shocked Americans and turned public opinion hostile to Germany, though not yet to the point of war.
war.source_title: American entry into World War I

war.text: President Woodrow Wilson made minimal preparations for a land war before 1917, though he did authorize a shipbuilding program for the United States Navy. He was narrowly re-elected in 1916 on an anti-war platform.
war.source_title: American entry into World War I

war.text: The phrase "American Century" was coined by Time publisher Henry Luce. In a February 17, 1941 Life magazine editorial, he urged the United States to forsake isolationism and enter World War II to defend democratic values.

In the 1941 State of the Union Address, known as the Four Freedoms speech, President Franklin D. Roosevelt broke with the tradition of non-interventionism. He outlined a US role in helping allies already at war. By August, he and Winston Churchill had drafted the Atlantic Charter to define goals for the post-war world.

In December 1941, Japan launched near-simultaneous offensives against Southeast Asia and the Central Pacific, including an attack on the US fleet at Pearl Harbor. The United States and United Kingdom declared war on Japan. Three days later, Germany and Italy declared war on the United States.
While the United States was still at peace, American banks made huge loans to the Entente powers. The money was used mainly to buy munitions, raw materials and food from the United States and Canada.
war.source_title: American entry into World War I

war.text: Of the three nuclear powers in NATO, only the United States has provided weapons for nuclear sharing. Canada hosted US nuclear weapons until 1984.

In 1914, Charleston interned a German freighter. When the freighter's skeleton crew tried to block Charleston harbor, they were all arrested and imprisoned. From then on, the city was buzzing with "war fever," and the low country coast around it was gripped by a mood that was very "pro-British and anti-German" through 1915, 1916 and early 1917. Southeast Georgia's newspapers meanwhile highlighted German atrocities such as the rape of Belgium and the execution of British nurse Edith Cavell.
war.source_title: American entry into World War I

war.text: Led by Governor Richard I. Manning, the South Carolina cities of Greenville, Spartanburg, and Columbia lobbied for army training centers in preparation for US entry into the war. They did so for both economic and patriotic reasons.
war.source_title: American entry into World War I

literature.text: Eugene O'Neill had more influence on American drama than any other dramatist in the early twentieth century. His first critical hit, Beyond the Horizon, debuted in 1920 and went on to win the Pulitzer Prize for Drama.

Eugene O'Neill was the most influential American dramatist of the early 20th century. His first critical hit, Beyond the Horizon, debuted in 1920 and won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama, and he later won it again for Anna Christie in 1922 and Strange Interlude in 1928.

The Poetry Collection at the University at Buffalo was founded in 1937 by Charles D. Abbott. It was the first institutional repository in the United States to systematically collect modern poetry and poets' working manuscripts, and it now holds over 140,000 titles, the largest poetry library of its kind in North America.

Eugene O'Neill wrote several plays for the Provincetown Players in New York City between 1916 and 1920. His later successes included Anna Christie, which won the Pulitzer Prize in 1922, and Strange Interlude, which won it in 1928.

Critic Kenneth Lincoln coined the term Native American Renaissance in his 1983 book of the same name. It described the sharp rise in literary works by Native Americans from the late 1960s onward, which followed the publication of Momaday's House Made of Dawn.

Joy Harjo of the Muscogee Nation became the first Native American U.S. Poet Laureate in April 2019. That same year Tommy Orange's There There was a finalist for the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction, and in 2021 Louise Erdrich won that prize for The Night Watchman.

American Indian literary nationalism holds that Native literatures should be read as the works of separate nations rather than as ethnic literature within the American canon. Simon J. Ortiz's 1981 essay is generally held to be its most significant precursor.

Charles Olson's 1950 essay Projective Verse called for poetry built on a line based on human breath. It became the foundation for the Black Mountain poets, who worked at Black Mountain College in North Carolina, and later influenced poets who moved to San Francisco.

Lincoln pointed out that a new generation of Native Americans was coming of age in the late 1960s and early 1970s. They were the first in their tribal communities to receive a substantial English-language education, particularly outside Indian boarding schools, and more of them graduated from colleges and universities. Conditions for Native people were still very harsh in this period, though they had moved beyond the survival conditions of the early half of the century.
Green Grow the Lilacs, a play by the Cherokee author Lynn Riggs, is perhaps the best-known Native American work of the early 20th century. It became the basis for the musical Oklahoma!

Louise Glück won the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry in 1993 for The Wild Iris. She is also the only living American author publishing primarily written poetry to have been awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature.

By the 1980s, Native American Studies programs at universities such as UCLA and Dartmouth had led to scholarly journals like SAIL and Wíčazo Ša Review, founded in 1985. Publishers also set up specialized imprints, including Harper and Row's Native American Publishing Programme, meant to promote new voices.

Robert Allen Warrior's Tribal Secrets was the first full-length work of nationalist criticism. Craig Womack's Red on Red was the first monograph to focus on the literature of a single tribal nation, leading some to call it tribalcentric.

science.text: Apollo 11 landed the first humans on the Moon in July 1969. Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on the lunar surface while Michael Collins stayed in orbit. Approximately 650 million people worldwide watched the first landing on television.

The Manhattan Project was a World War II program to produce the first nuclear weapons. Led by the United States with the United Kingdom and Canada, it employed nearly 130,000 people at its peak and cost nearly US$2 billion.

Jonas Salk's polio vaccine was announced as safe on April 12, 1955, and he was hailed as a "miracle worker." He chose not to patent it or seek any profit, in order to maximize its global distribution.

ENIAC, completed in 1945, was the first programmable, electronic, general-purpose digital computer. It was designed by John Mauchly and J. Presper Eckert to calculate artillery firing tables for the U.S. Army. The press called it a "Giant Brain."

The first working transistor was a point-contact device invented in 1947 by John Bardeen, Walter Brattain and William Shockley at Bell Labs. They shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics. Transistors paved the way for smaller and cheaper radios, calculators and computers.

The Human Genome Project began officially in 1990 and was declared complete on 14 April 2003. It was the world's largest collaborative biological project. Funding came from the US government through the National Institutes of Health, among other groups.

After successful tests on laboratory animals, Jonas Salk injected 43 children with his killed-virus vaccine on July 2, 1952, at the D.T. Watson Home for Crippled Children in Sewickley, Pennsylvania. A few weeks later he injected children at the Polk State School for the Retarded and Feeble-minded. He vaccinated his own children in 1953, and in 1954 he tested the vaccine on about one million children, known as the polio pioneers.
tags: D.T. Watson Home for Crippled Children

science.text: Before Salk's vaccine, polio had struck the U.S. in huge waves: in 1952 and 1953 there were 58,000 and 35,000 cases, with 3,200 and 1,400 deaths. After Salk's vaccine was licensed in 1955, a mass immunization campaign promoted by the March of Dimes began. Annual cases fell from 35,000 in 1953 to 5,600 by 1957, and by 1961 only 161 cases were recorded. In 1955 the Cutter company's improperly inactivated vaccine caused 260 cases of polio, killing 11 children.

After moving to Pacific Grove, California, Isabella Abbott studied the algae of the California coast and adapted recipes to use local bull kelp (Nereocystis) in foods such as cakes and pickles. She later compiled a book on the marine algae of the Monterey peninsula, which was expanded to cover the whole California coast.

Plutonium for the Manhattan Project was produced in the world's first industrial-scale nuclear reactors at the Hanford Engineer Works in Washington. Because of high radioactivity, work in the separation plants was done by remote control using closed-circuit television, something unheard of in 1943.

ENIAC's first program was a study of the feasibility of the thermonuclear weapon. Its conception began in June 1941, when John Mauchly supervised graduate students computing artillery firing tables and wondered whether electronics could speed the work. The project was built in secret under the code name "Project PX."

By 1972, Stanford University promoted Isabella Abbott directly to full professor of biology, where she was the first woman and first person of color in that position. In 1997 she received the Gilbert Morgan Smith Medal from the National Academy of Sciences.

In 1997, Herbert Ratner of Oak Park, Illinois, gave researcher Michele Carbone vials of the 1955 Salk vaccine that he had kept in a refrigerator for over forty years. Testing showed they contained the SV40 monkey virus, including a slow-growing strain also found in some malignant tumors and lymphomas.

politics.text: The American Century is the idea that the period since the middle of the 20th century has been largely dominated by the United States in political, economic, technological and cultural terms. After the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, the United States remained the world's only superpower.

The United States entered World War I in 1917 as a self-styled "Associated Power" and was never formally a member of the Allies. President Woodrow Wilson argued that the war was so important that the US had to have a voice in the peace conference.
The war ended in 1919 with the Treaty of Versailles, but the United States then turned to isolationism. It refused to endorse the treaty or formally enter the League of Nations.

When World War II began in 1939, Canada was one of four independent Dominions to join the war alongside the United Kingdom. Britain made heavy purchases of munitions and supplies in Canada, and Canada also made gifts.
politics.source_title: British Empire in World War II

politics.text: The Smoot–Hawley Tariff Act, passed during the interwar years of economic protectionism, is credited by economists with prolonging and spreading the Great Depression. From 1934, trade liberalization began under the Reciprocal Trade Agreements Act.

In 1940 the United States ranked only 18th in military power, and American public opinion remained isolationist. The 800,000-member America First Committee vehemently opposed intervention in Europe, even as the US sold military aid to the United Kingdom and the Soviet Union through Lend-Lease.

The Dakota Access Pipeline was built in 2016 through unceded Oceti Sakowin territory, and the #NoDAPL protests followed. During the protests the National Guard and Emergency Management Assistant Compact were deployed to suppress resistance and often resorted to violence. The pipeline was completed in 2017 despite the protests. Within six months it had leaked five times, and two major incidents in 2017 and 2019 spilled a total of 800,000 gallons.
politics.source_title: Native American genocide in the United States

philosophy.text: American philosophy since the 20th century is mostly analytic philosophy, with W. V. O. Quine and Saul Kripke among its most prominent figures. World War I and World War II crystalized the split between analytic and continental philosophy. Existentialism and phenomenology, though very popular in Europe, never reached the same popularity in America.

Native American religions include a wide range of Indigenous spiritual practices, passed down through myths, oral histories, stories, allegories and principles. A series of federal laws banned traditional practices such as feasts, Sun Dance ceremonies and the sweat lodge, and government persecution and prosecution continued until 1978, when the American Indian Religious Freedom Act was passed. Native children were also removed from their families into government-funded, church-run boarding schools, where they were forced through violence and oppression to learn European Christian beliefs and the English language, and were forbidden to speak their own languages or practice their own beliefs. This system continued through the 1970s, and it has been argued that the act had little real effect on protecting Native religious beliefs.

The Native American Church, also known as Peyotism, teaches a combination of traditional Native American beliefs and elements of Christianity, with sacramental use of peyote. Today it is the most widespread indigenous religion among Native Americans in the United States, Canada and Mexico, with an estimated 300,000 adherents.
H. L. Mencken introduced Friedrich Nietzsche to America with The Philosophy of Friedrich Nietzsche in 1908. He thought Nietzsche's philosophy was exemplified by Theodore Roosevelt.

Susanne Langer wrote a theory of symbolism in Philosophy in a New Key in 1942, the same year Van Meter Ames started the American Society for Aesthetics. Morris Weitz argued that necessary and sufficient conditions will never exist for the concept 'art', because it is an "open concept".

Arthur Danto and George Dickie argued for the artworld, or an "institutional definition of art". Dickie's student Noël Carroll contributes to the philosophy of film. Jerrold Levinson best exemplifies a rival approach, the historical definition of art.

In 1968, several Ojibwe Natives founded the American Indian Movement, which soon gained a Lakota focus. In 1973 its members occupied Wounded Knee and were besieged by U.S. federal authorities. AIM politicized Lakota religion, turning it into a symbol of resistance, and converted the sacred pipe into a Pan-Indian symbol.

The Half-Moon way of the Native American Church was introduced in 1914 or 1924 by James Seymour, of the Winnebago tribe. In the Cross-fire way a Bible is placed on an altar and baptism is practiced. In the Half-Moon way no Bible is used and there is no baptism.
Kendall Walton formulated a "make-believe" theory of representation. It influenced the fields of anti-realist ontology and aesthetics.

culture.text: Religion in the United States is both widespread and diverse, with higher reported levels of belief than other wealthy Western nations. Christianity is the most widely professed religion, though as of 2012 Protestants no longer formed a majority in the US.

Canada, Mexico, and the United States jointly hosted the 2026 FIFA World Cup. The United States and Canada also have major sports teams that compete against each other in baseball, basketball, hockey, and soccer.

Native American literature saw a surge in the late 1960s, which critic Kenneth Lincoln named the Native American Renaissance in a 1983 book. The term came to describe the flowering of literary works that followed N. Scott Momaday's House Made of Dawn in 1968.

Among the Lakota, the sacred pipe, sweat lodge purification ceremony, vision quest, and sun dance are important rituals. Seven of the rituals are presented as having been given by a benevolent spirit, White Buffalo Calf Woman.

In 1938, a radio broadcast of The War of the Worlds, directed and narrated by Orson Welles, caused a sensation. It convinced part of the general public that a Martian invasion was ongoing. It was set in contemporary America and presented as a live news story happening in New Jersey.

Black Elk, an Oglála holy man, dictated his beliefs to John G. Neihardt and Joseph Epes Brown, and these were first published as Black Elk Speaks in 1932. He was committed to both traditional Lakota religion and Catholicism.
Scandinavia House opened in 2000 in Manhattan as the American-Scandinavian Foundation's cultural center. It was designed by architect James Stewart Polshek and cost around $13 million to build.
culture.source_title: Scandinavia House – The Nordic Center in America

culture.text: The American Indian Movement was founded in 1968 by several Ojibwe Natives and soon gained a Lakota focus. In 1973 its members occupied Wounded Knee and were besieged by federal authorities. AIM turned Lakota religion into a symbol of resistance, and by the early 21st century the sweat lodge ceremony had spread to indigenous communities across North America.

The Native American Church combines traditional Native American beliefs with elements of Christianity and the sacramental use of peyote. The Half-Moon way was introduced in 1914 or 1924 by James Seymour of the Winnebago tribe. In that way no Bible, baptism, or minister is used, unlike the Cross-fire way.

In 1916, Eugene O'Neill began writing plays for the Provincetown Players, and he later won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama for Anna Christie in 1922 and Strange Interlude in 1928. His Long Day's Journey into Night was published after his death and is often regarded as one of the finest American plays of the twentieth century.

A Gallup poll in 2007 found that 53% of Americans would refuse to vote for an atheist as president, up from 48% in 1987 and 1999. The share then dropped to a record low of 43% in 2012 and 40% in 2015.

Federal rulings such as US v. Boyll (1991) and the Religious Freedom Restoration Act of 1993 allow members of the Native American Church to possess and use peyote for religious purposes, despite the 1970 Controlled Substances Act. Only enrolled tribal members with a permit can buy peyote from licensed distributors, which are located in Texas near the Mexican border.
